questions.prompt: What is the derivative of f(x) = sin(x)?
questions.explanation: d/dx[sin(x)] = cos(x). The cosine function is the derivative of sine.

questions.prompt: What is the derivative of f(x) = e^x?
questions.explanation: e^x is its own derivative — a unique property that makes it central in calculus and ML.

questions.prompt: What is ∫ (1/x) dx?
questions.explanation: The antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x|, valid for x ≠ 0.

questions.prompt: What does the second derivative of a function tell you?

options.text: The concavity / rate of change of the slope

questions.explanation: f''(x) measures how the slope itself is changing — positive means concave up, negative concave down.

questions.prompt: What is the product rule for d/dx[f(x)·g(x)]?
questions.explanation: The product rule: differentiate one factor at a time and sum the results.

questions.prompt: What is the derivative of f(x) = ln(x)?
questions.explanation: d/dx[ln(x)] = 1/x for x > 0.

questions.prompt: Using the limit definition, the derivative of f at x is:
questions.explanation: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient as h approaches zero.

questions.prompt: At a local maximum of a smooth function, what is true?
questions.explanation: At any smooth local extremum, the first derivative is zero (a critical point).

questions.prompt: The difference between a definite and an indefinite integral is:

options.text: Definite has limits and returns a number; indefinite returns a function + C
Definite only works with trig functions

questions.explanation: Definite integrals evaluate over an interval [a, b] and yield a number; indefinite integrals yield a family of antiderivatives.

questions.prompt: In multivariate calculus, ∂f/∂x measures:

options.text: The rate of change of f with respect to x, holding other variables constant
The integral of f over x

questions.explanation: Partial derivatives isolate the effect of one variable, treating the others as constants — the foundation of gradient descent.

questions.prompt: The main difference between K-means and K-medoids is:

options.text: K-medoids uses actual data points as cluster centers

questions.explanation: K-medoids picks real samples (medoids) as representatives, making it more robust to outliers than K-means' means.

questions.prompt: The elbow method is used to:

options.text: Choose the number of clusters K

questions.explanation: Plot within-cluster variance vs K; look for the 'elbow' where adding clusters stops helping much.

questions.prompt: The silhouette score ranges from:
questions.explanation: Silhouette measures how similar a point is to its own cluster vs the nearest other cluster. Values near 1 mean well-separated clusters; near -1 means likely misassigned.

questions.prompt: Hierarchical clustering produces:
questions.explanation: Hierarchical clustering builds a dendrogram; you cut it at a chosen height to get the final clusters.

questions.prompt: Agglomerative vs divisive hierarchical clustering:

options.text: Agglomerative merges bottom-up; divisive splits top-down

questions.explanation: Agglomerative starts with each point as its own cluster and merges; divisive starts with one big cluster and splits.

questions.prompt: Why is K-means sensitive to feature scaling?

options.text: It uses Euclidean distance, so large-range features dominate

questions.explanation: Distance-based methods treat every unit equally — a feature on a 0–1 scale can't compete with one on a 0–10000 scale.

questions.prompt: K-means++ is a variant that:

options.text: Spreads out initial centroids to reduce bad local optima

questions.explanation: K-means++ picks initial centroids far apart, avoiding poor local minima that random init often falls into.

questions.prompt: Which clustering method is most appropriate for finding arbitrarily shaped, density-based clusters with outliers?
questions.explanation: DBSCAN groups dense regions and labels sparse points as noise — no assumption of spherical clusters.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a common internal clustering validation metric?
questions.explanation: RMSE measures regression error against labels. The other three evaluate cluster quality without ground-truth labels.

questions.prompt: K-means iteratively does which two steps?

options.text: Assign points to nearest centroid, then recompute centroids
Sample data, then train a neural net

questions.explanation: Each iteration: (1) assign every point to its nearest centroid; (2) move each centroid to the mean of its assigned points.

questions.prompt: In a Conv layer, 'stride' controls:

options.text: How far the filter moves each step

questions.explanation: Stride 2 halves the output spatial size (before padding). Larger strides reduce computation.

questions.prompt: Max pooling is used to:

options.text: Downsample feature maps by taking the max in each window

questions.explanation: Max pooling reduces spatial dimensions, adds translation invariance, and has no learnable parameters.

questions.prompt: A Conv layer with C_in=64, C_out=128, kernel 3×3 has how many weight parameters (ignoring bias)?
questions.explanation: Each of the 128 output channels has its own 3×3×64 kernel. Total: 3·3·64·128 = 73,728.

questions.prompt: The 'receptive field' of a neuron refers to:

options.text: The region of the input it can 'see'

questions.explanation: The receptive field grows with depth — deep neurons 'see' larger regions of the original image.

questions.prompt: A 1×1 convolution is useful for:
questions.explanation: 1×1 convs blend information across channels without affecting spatial dimensions — used to reduce or expand channel counts cheaply.

questions.prompt: Why is batch normalization often used in CNNs?

options.text: To stabilize and speed up training by normalizing activations
To reduce the number of filters

questions.explanation: BatchNorm normalizes each mini-batch's activations, allowing higher learning rates and reducing sensitivity to initialization.

questions.prompt: Transfer learning with a pretrained CNN typically means:

options.text: Retraining from scratch on new data
Reusing early layers and fine-tuning later layers

questions.explanation: Early layers capture generic features (edges, textures). You freeze them and fine-tune the later, task-specific layers.

questions.prompt: Which is a data augmentation technique for image CNNs?
questions.explanation: Augmentation artificially expands the training set by applying label-preserving transforms like flips, rotations, crops, and color jitter.

questions.prompt: A CNN typically ends with fully connected layers because:

options.text: They can combine global features into class scores

questions.explanation: After convolutional feature extraction, FC layers mix all spatial information to produce final predictions.

questions.prompt: Padding with zeros before a conv layer is typically used to:

options.text: Preserve spatial dimensions and edge information

questions.explanation: 'Same' padding keeps output size close to input and lets filters process border pixels.

questions.prompt: Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV):

options.text: Uses each sample as the validation set once

questions.explanation: LOOCV trains n models for n samples — extremely expensive but nearly unbiased on small datasets.

questions.prompt: Stratified K-fold differs from regular K-fold because:

options.text: It preserves class proportions in each fold

questions.explanation: Stratification ensures each fold has roughly the same class balance — critical for imbalanced datasets.

questions.prompt: For time-series data, standard K-fold CV is inappropriate because:

options.text: It uses future data to predict the past, causing data leakage

questions.explanation: Time-series CV must respect chronology — use expanding-window or rolling-origin splits.

questions.prompt: Nested cross-validation is used to:

options.text: Get an unbiased estimate when hyperparameters are also being tuned

questions.explanation: Inner CV tunes hyperparameters; outer CV evaluates generalization. Standard CV that tunes inside leaks information into the score.

questions.prompt: Bayesian optimization for hyperparameter tuning:

options.text: Models the objective and picks promising configurations

questions.explanation: It builds a probabilistic model (typically a Gaussian process) of the objective to choose the next configuration to evaluate.

questions.prompt: Early stopping is a form of:
questions.explanation: Halting when validation loss stops improving prevents overfitting — a form of implicit regularization.

questions.prompt: Grid search vs random search with the same budget:

options.text: Random often wins because most hyperparameters don't matter and random explores more

questions.explanation: When only a few hyperparameters matter, random search covers more useful values along those dimensions.

questions.prompt: Cross-validation reduces the risk of overfitting the test set because:

options.text: Every sample serves as validation once, giving a more reliable estimate

questions.explanation: A single train/val split is high-variance; CV averages over multiple splits.

questions.prompt: Group K-fold is appropriate when:

options.text: Samples form groups (e.g., patients) that must not be split across folds

questions.explanation: If samples from the same group appear in both train and validation, the model can memorize group identity — a leak.

questions.prompt: A learning curve plots:

options.text: Training and validation error vs training set size

questions.explanation: Learning curves reveal whether you need more data (both curves converge high) or a better model (large train/val gap).

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quicksort?
questions.explanation: With poorly chosen pivots (e.g., already sorted input + first-element pivot), Quicksort degrades to O(n²).

questions.prompt: A hash collision occurs when:

options.text: Two keys map to the same hash slot

questions.explanation: Collisions are handled by chaining (linked lists) or open addressing (probing).

questions.prompt: BFS vs DFS: which uses a queue?
questions.explanation: BFS explores level by level using a queue; DFS uses a stack (or recursion).

questions.prompt: In a binary tree, 'in-order' traversal visits nodes in the order:
questions.explanation: In-order: recurse left, visit root, recurse right. For a BST, this yields sorted order.

questions.prompt: Dynamic programming is best suited for problems that have:
questions.explanation: DP caches subproblem solutions. It shines when the same subproblems repeat across the recursion tree.

questions.prompt: Greedy algorithms differ from DP because:

options.text: Greedy commits to local choices without revisiting

questions.explanation: Greedy makes the locally best choice at each step; DP considers all subproblems. Greedy is faster when the greedy choice is provably optimal.

questions.prompt: In a min-heap, what is the time complexity of extracting the minimum?
questions.explanation: Extracting the root is O(1) to peek but requires O(log n) to restore the heap property by sifting down.

questions.prompt: Every recursive function must have:

options.text: A base case that stops recursion

questions.explanation: Without a base case, recursion never terminates and overflows the call stack.

questions.prompt: Compared to arrays, linked lists:

options.text: Offer O(1) insert/delete at known positions but O(n) random access

questions.explanation: Linked lists trade random access for cheap insertions/deletions at a known node.

questions.prompt: A 'space-time tradeoff' in algorithms means:

options.text: Using more memory can reduce runtime, and vice versa

questions.explanation: Caching, hash tables, and DP tables are classic examples: extra memory buys faster lookups or avoids recomputation.
